SK1110 Collapse the forwarding overload into an optional parameter

A non-public overload whose whole body forwards to a longer one, passing its own parameters straight through and a constant for the extra, is an optional parameter written as a second method.

CategoryModernization
Default severitysuggestion
ScopeSemantic
Needs a compilationyes
Runs under --load=looseno
Cached per fileyes
Fixyes, review it
Language version floor—
Since2.0
ReSharperRedundantOverload.Local (resharper_redundant_overload_local_highlighting)

Why

Two declarations, two doc comments and two places to change say one thing: the last argument has a default. The optional parameter says it once, in the signature, where a reader looking at the method finds it — and where the caller's tooling shows it, which the forwarding overload never does. It is also a shape a model produces constantly, because optional parameters postdate a great deal of the C# in its training data and writing the second overload is what the older dialect required.

Example

Instead of:

string Render(string text) => Render(text, 4);

string Render(string text, int indent) => new string(' ', indent) + text;

Write:

string Render(string text, int indent = 4) => new string(' ', indent) + text;

When it does not fire

⚠ Restricted to what is not externally visible, and that restriction is the rule rather than a caution attached to it. An optional parameter's default is compiled into every call site, so changing it later does not reach callers that were already built, and deleting an overload from a published surface is a binary break outright — RedundantOverload.Global is the half of the ReSharper pair that carries this hazard, and issue #112 asks for .Local to ship alone. Effective accessibility is computed by walking the containing types, so a public method on an internal class is treated as internal and is reported, while a public method on a public class is not; protected counts as externally visible and is declined. ⚠ The forwarding overload may exist on purpose, and the signals that say so withdraw the finding. Any attribute on it is taken as intent — [Obsolete], [EditorBrowsable], [DllImport] and every test-framework marker say the declaration is doing a job the body does not show. virtual, override, abstract, partial and any implementation of an interface member are declined, because the overload's existence may be a contract rather than a convenience. ⚠ Exactly two methods of that name, or nothing. Deleting one overload changes which candidate wins for every call that used it, and with a third overload in the set the new winner need not be the one the body forwarded to. Requiring the pair makes the outcome decidable by reading the two declarations. ⚠ The forwarded argument must be a compile-time constant, asked of the semantic model rather than pattern-matched on the syntax, because only a constant can become a default. Render(text, text.Length) is a different method, not a defaulted one, and is silent. ⚠ The extra parameter must be last and must not already be optional or `params`, since C# admits no optional parameter after a params and none before a required one. The pass-through must be positional, in order, name for name: a call that reorders, renames, wraps or converts an argument is doing work, and the rule only recognises the identity forwarding. A body that does anything besides the single forwarding return — a log line, a guard, a null check — is declined, since the extra statement would be deleted with the method. Generic methods are excluded on either side. A comment inside the deleted declaration, or a preprocessor directive anywhere in it, withdraws the finding; the method's own documentation comment is deleted with it, which is intended, and leading trivia holding anything other than whitespace and that documentation is declined. Marked unsafe because the fix deletes a declaration: within an assembly the change is source-compatible and the compiler proves it, but what a reviewer must confirm is that the overload was a convenience and not a promise.
